blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: We ask how much of a transformer's backbone the Chorus N-gram module replaces. Chorus adds hashed tables of token bigrams and trigrams to its input and attention. We train models of 16M to 349M parameters on 1.34 billion tokens of Polish printed before 1918 and find the size of a plain model with the same held-out loss. A separate learning-rate search for each kind of model cuts Chorus's gain at 47M by about a third. With tables about as large as the backbone, Chorus then matches a plain model 1.34 times its size at 16M and 1.16 to 1.20 times from 107M to 349M. With these tables, each added parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters. Chorus trains slower than a plain model of its size and faster than one of the same loss. On a fact quiz the two differ about as much as two seeds of one model. The results rest on one corpus, one 8,000-token vocabulary and a fifth of an epoch.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Lookup memories give a language model more parameters with little added computation per token.
Engram ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) reads hashed N-gram embeddings into the residual stream, and Chorus ( Chung and Du, 2026a ) shares one set of N-gram tables between the input and the attention values of
many layers. Chung and Du vary Chorus’s tables from 20M to 9.6B parameters on a backbone of 21M and train one table
size each on backbones of 17M and 133M.
Someone choosing a model needs to know how many backbone parameters a table of a given size replaces,
and whether that number changes with the size of the backbone.

blocks.en:
We measure this number for Chorus at five backbone sizes, from 16M to 349M parameters, on the
Wieszcz-XIX corpus of Polish printed before 1918 ( Kocur, 2026 ) . We call the transformer
that Chorus is added to the backbone, and the same transformer trained without Chorus the plain model.
For each Chorus model we read off the size a plain model needs for the same held-out loss, its
equivalent size. A learning rate shared by both kinds of model can favour one of them, so we search the
rate at every size for each kind separately. Section 4 reports the effect of the rate
search, equivalent sizes at several token budgets, larger tables, the parts of the module, a fact quiz and
training throughput.

blocks.en: 2 Related work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Several recent modules add parameters that are looked up by
token or by a hash of the last few tokens. Engram ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) , called Deep Sparse Embedding
in the proceedings version, reads such embeddings into a mixture-of-experts model. The Over-Tokenized
Transformer ( Huang et al., 2025a ) grows the input vocabulary with them and reports that its 400M
model with the largest vocabulary matches the training loss of a 1B model without it. The count tables
of COUNT, held in host memory ( Magnusson et al., 2026 ) , keep statistics of the training data outside
the network. Appendix G lists further work of this kind.

blocks.en:
Scaling studies relate loss to model size and data ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) , and untuned learning rates distort such
comparisons ( Porian et al., 2024 ) . N-gram tables added to a pretrained 0.6B model brought no gain
at the backbone’s rate and were trained at fifty times that rate ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . The value of
added parameters has been given as the size of an equivalent dense model for routed models ( Clark et al., 2022 ) , and memory layers outperform dense models with more than twice their
computation ( Berges et al., 2025 ) . JTok ( Yang et al., 2026b ) reports the computation a

rStation ( 2026b ) , where agents also report dense-equivalent multipliers of hashed
N-gram input tables of 151k rows, about × \times 1.3 at 26M and × \times 1.2 at 135M, with one fixed recipe ( 2026a ) . The Over-Tokenized Transformer and COUNT each give their gain
across model sizes as an equivalent size or as computation, with one training recipe for models with
and without tables. To our knowledge, as of November 2026, no published work measures the equivalent
size of a learned N-gram memory with the backbone’s learning rate searched at every size for both
kinds of model.

blocks.en: 3.1 Data

blocks.en:
All models train on the training split of the Wieszcz-XIX corpus ( Kocur, 2026 ) , 6.69

training side. A full run reads 1.34 billion tokens at random positions
of the training split, a fifth of an epoch. Appendix C gives the exact counts.

blocks.en:
The backbone is a decoder-only transformer with rotary position embeddings, RMSNorm before each
sublayer and on its output, QK-normalisation, a SwiGLU feed-forward layer, grouped-query attention, a
context of 1,024 tokens and input embeddings tied to the output head. The six sizes follow one rule:
the width is 48 times the number of layers, the head dimension is 64, and there are a third as many
key/value heads as query heads (Table 1 ).

blocks.en: 3.3 Chorus
blocks.zh: 3.3 声调

blocks.en:
We reimplement Chorus as described by Chung and Du (2026a) , following their code. For each token, the module
looks up one row in each of four shared N-gram tables, two for bigrams and two for trigrams, and one
row in a token table. The key of an N-gram is its token ids read as one number in base 8,001, the
extra symbol marking a position before the start of the sequence. A table’s row is that key modulo its
number of rows, which is m m , m + 2 m+2 , m + 4 m+4 or m + 6 m+6 for a size m m set by the table budget. Each N-gram row has a quarter of the model’s width;
joined, they are added to the token row of the full width. A sigmoid gate computed from the last three
token embeddings scales the result, and a causal depthwise convolution over four positions refines it.
The result is added once to the input embedding and, through a projection gated by each block’s hidden
state, to the attention values of the even-numbered blocks. The tables start at zero, so an untrained module leaves the
backbone unchanged.

blocks.en: 3.4 Training
blocks.zh: 3.4 培训

blocks.en:
A full run takes 5,104 steps of 262,144 tokens (256 sequences of 1,024) with a warmup of 300
steps. The rate then stays at its peak and falls linearly to a tenth of it over the last 10% of
steps, a short form of the cooldown studied by Hägele et al. (2024) . Runs at half and
twice the budget resume a full run from a step still at the peak rate and cool down over their own
last 10% of steps. Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) trains the two-dimensional weights of the blocks and of the module, AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) the embedding, the normalisation weights and the convolution, and SparseAdam the tables.

windows of 1,024 tokens spread evenly over the held-out split, in float32 . Every model is

and 23 configurations at 16M, 47M, 107M, 204M and 349M also with further seeds (Table 8 ).

spread. A plain and a Chorus model with the same seed read different training positions, since the module

blocks.en: 5 Summary
blocks.zh: 5 总结

blocks.en:
With the backbone’s rate searched for both kinds of model and the tables’ rate fixed, Chorus with
equal-size tables reaches the loss of a plain model × \times 1.34 its size at 16M
and × \times 1.16 to × \times 1.20 its size from 107M to
349M. Each parameter added by equal-size or larger tables replaces at most
0.31 backbone parameters, so at the
same total number of parameters a plain model reaches a lower loss, at more computation per token. With a tables’ rate of 0.0005 instead of 0.0015, the multipliers are
0.02 to 0.07 higher and still fall with size. In single-seed runs at half the budget, of two backbones that see about as many tokens per
parameter, the larger has the lower multiplier. Larger
tables raise the multiplier, but the 47M model with 1.07 billion parameters still has a higher loss
than the 107M plain model. A Chorus model with equal-size tables trains 3 to 11% faster than a plain model of the same
loss, against a run-to-run spread of up to 3%.

We round every row of the tables, the token table included, to signed integers of a given width, with
the row’s largest magnitude as its 16-bit scale, and measure the change in held-out loss on 1,024
windows spread over the held-out split (Table 9 ). Stored in eight bits, the tables
change the loss by 0.000 nats. In four bits the change is 0.002 nats, at about

is 0.012 to 0.014 nats, and in two bits 0.186 to 0.235, more than the tables gave. Chung and Du (2026b) report more than 99% of the gain of generic N-gram tables kept at four bits,
as a share of the tables’ own gain; ours is a share of the whole module’s gain, at the base rate.
